newsitem.title: USA: U.S. helping Iraqi dissidents flee, Clinton says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. helping Iraqi dissidents flee, Clinton says.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Monday the United States is helping "those who have worked with us" to flee Iraq amid Kurdish strife that reportedly wrecked a CIA effort to topple Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
"We're doing everything we think we can to help anyone who needs to be out of Iraq," Clinton told reporters.

He declined to elaborate, but he was responding to a question about some 200 Iraqi Arabs with links to the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency who reportedly fled the Kurdish city of Arbil after Iraqi troops stormed it last week.
The Iraqi intervention prompted U.S. retaliation in the form of cruise missile strikes against anti-aircraft defences and expansion of a no-fly zone in the south of Iraq.

The Washington Post reported on Monday that the Kurdish opponents of Saddam in the Arbil region, members of the CIA-funded Iraqi National Congress, are holed up in a mountain hideout in northern Iraq fearing for their lives and hoping for U.S. political asylum.
About 100 of their colleagues were arrested by Iraqi secret police and apparently executed after Arbil was overrun, Iraqi dissidents said.

"We're doing everything we can to get out of Iraq American citizens and those who have worked with us," Clinton said. "As to the intelligence matters, I can't comment, but we are doing everything that we can do and we believe is appropriate."
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole said the disarray among anti-Saddam forces was one of several factors that caused him to doubt the effectiveness of Clinton's strategy toward Iraq.

"The reports of continued strife and killings in Northern Iraq -- to include execution of U.S.-backed Iraqi opposition personnel, the apparent entrenchment of Iraqi troops around Arbil, and the lack of evidence of an Iraqi withdrawal from the North raise questions about whether the administration's strategy has advanced US interests in the region," Dole said.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said all Americans who had been in northern Iraq -- "a variety of people doing a variety of things" -- had left after the Iraqi onslaught that prompted the U.S. missile strikes.
Burns, speaking at a regular news briefing, said the United States had spoken to a number of countries about the possibility of helping those threatened by Iraqi forces in the Kurdish enclave.

Rend Rahim Francke of the Washington-based Iraq Foundation, a U.S. government-subsidised group working for democracy in Iraq, said the Saddam opponents sheltering in the mountain resort of Salahuddin were in "grave danger."
She said the group totalled as many 600, including family members of the 200 Iraqi National Congress members.
"Saddam's intelligence and security are all over the area, and these people are probably highly wanted by the Iraqi authorities," Francke said, adding many were army defectors.

Clinton said the fighting in northern Iraq, which brought Baghdad's intervention and the U.S. retaliation last week, was confined primarily to Kurdish factions. The State Department said Monday it was in touch with the factions and had urged them to halt hostilities.

Clinton reportedly expanded the covert anti-Saddam operation in January, signing a secret order directing the CIA to provide weapons and training and to install intelligence-gathering equipment for Saddam's foes.
The CIA declined comment on the setback to its operation, said by experts to be the biggest U.S. covert operation since aiding anti-Soviet guerrillas in Afghanistan in the 1980s.
Helping rescue Iraqis who worked with the CIA would normally be a high priority for operational reasons as well as for moral ones, experts said.

"They don't want these guys to be captured and tortured" for fear they would disclose more secrets, said Kenneth Katzman, a former CIA analyst who tracks Iraq and Iran at the Congressional Research Service.
